# Abstract

The Maurya Empire (322BC to 185BC) represented the first continental state in South Asian history, integrating approximately 3,94M km² (3.938.787 km²) from the Hindu Kush and Indus drainage eastward across the Indo-Gangetic alluvium to the Bengal delta, and southward across the Malwa plateau, the Deccan and the Krishna-Tungabhadra basins. At its territorial and demographic apex under Ashoka Maurya around 260BC, the empire commanded an estimated 47M inhabitants (bounded between 43,24M and 50,76M), yielding an aggregate continental density of 1.193,26 persons per 100 km² (11,93 persons per km²). This vast demographic scale was anchored by the alluvial heartland of Prachya and the Magadhan core, which concentrated 17,86M people (38% of the imperial total) across the middle and lower Ganga valley at a density of 1.900,42 persons per 100 km², flanked by densely populated coastal deltas in Kalinga (3,76M, 2.445,86 persons per 100 km²) and the agrarian-commercial viceroyalties of Uttarapatha (8,93M), Avantiratha (7,99M) and Dakshinapatha (8,46M).

The structural cohesion of the Mauryan state rested upon a deliberate dual mechanism of administrative integration and agronomic expansion documented in Kautilya's *Arthashastra* and corroborated by the distribution of Ashokan edicts, punch-marked silver currency (*karshapana*) and Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW) ceramic assemblages. Through state-directed rural colonisation (*janapadanivesha*), the imperial administration transferred surplus populations from congested urban districts and prisoner-of-war contingents onto crown lands (*sita*), providing draught oxen, seed grain and tax exemptions to transform deciduous forests and riverine savannahs into settled agricultural tax bases. The state actively constructed and regulated reservoir and canal irrigation works (*setubandha*), secured long-distance trunk routes such as the *rajapatha* linking Pataliputra to Taxila, and established royal storehouses (*kosthagara*) to buffer provincial populations against seasonal drought and crop failure.

This historical demographic reconstruction combines 9.518 catalogued settlement trajectories (fitting a Zipf rank-size slope of $\alpha = 0,87$, $R^2 = 0,95$) with systematic spatial kriging, environmental suitability models and epigraphic mapping across five canonical imperial viceroyalties: Prachya and the Magadhan core (3.414 settlements), Uttarapatha (2.203), Dakshinapatha (2.084), Avantiratha (1.440) and Kalinga (377). Reconstructed population expanded from 39M in 322BC following Chandragupta Maurya's overthrow of the Nanda dynasty and annexation of the northwestern satrapies from Seleucus Nicator, rising to 42,5M in 300BC, attaining 47M at the time of the Kalinga conquest in 260BC, and peaking at 48,5M around 230BC towards the close of Ashoka's reign. Following Ashoka's death and subsequent dynastic partition among regional governors, administrative cohesion loosened, leading to modest regional contractions and frontier secession that brought the population to 46,5M by the fall of the dynasty in 185BC. By isolating nucleated urban centres from rural peasantries through settlement subtraction, INDUS reconstructs an authentic archaeological baseline for the ancient South Asian demographic transition.

# Imperial Administration and Provincial Viceroyalties

## The Five Ashokan Provinces

The administrative architecture of the Maurya Empire was organised around a central imperial territory governed directly from Pataliputra and four outlying viceroyalties (*cakra*) administered by royal princes (*aryaputra* or *kumara*) assisted by councils of ministers (*mahamatras*) [@Fauconnier2015Occidente; @Dwivedi2021Territoria]. Following the conquest of Kalinga around 261BC, a fifth provincial seat was incorporated at Tosali, creating a fivefold regional division reflected in Ashokan epigraphy (Table \ref{tab:subregions}):

### Uttarapatha (Taxila Viceroyalty, Indus and Punjab)

The northwestern province of Uttarapatha (1.093.083 km², 27,75% of imperial area) encompassed the Punjab alluvial plains, the Potohar plateau, the Peshawar basin, the lower Indus valley of Sindh, and the frontier satrapies of Paropamisadae, Arachosia and Gedrosia ceded to Chandragupta by Seleucus I Nicator around 303BC [@Morris2019Central; @Morris2019Evidence]. Headquartered at the ancient metropolis of Taxila (Bhir Mound), Uttarapatha functioned as the primary strategic gateway connecting the Indian subcontinent with the Hellenistic kingdoms of Central Asia and the Iranian plateau [@Fauconnier2015Occidente].

Agricultural settlement in Uttarapatha relied upon inundation canals and riverine terraces flanking the Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi and Sutlej rivers [@Kumar2025Investigat; @Possehl1999IndusAge; @Kenoyer1998AncientCities]. Population within the province rose from 7,41M in 322BC to 8,08M in 300BC and reached 8,93M at the imperial apex in 260BC, with an average density of 816,96 persons per 100 km². Across 2.203 catalogued settlements in the province, major nucleated urban centres included Taxila (59,1k peak in 185BC; 53,6k in 260BC), Charsadda (Pushkalavati, 35,6k peak in 185BC), Sialkot (34,1k peak in 185BC), Delhi (Indraprastha, 28,1k peak in 185BC), Multan (24,4k peak in 185BC) and Peshawar (19,2k peak in 185BC), serving as critical hubs along the northern trade route [@Allchin1995Archaeology; @Morris2019Evidence].

### Prachya and the Magadhan Core (Pataliputra, Ganga Valley and Bengal)

The central and eastern province of Prachya (939.790 km², 23,86% of imperial area) constituted the demographic, economic and political heart of the empire. Stretching from the Ganga-Yamuna doab eastward across the middle Ganga plains of Bihar, the fertile floodplains of North and South Bengal, and the Brahmaputra margins, this province encompassed the ancestral territory of Magadha [@Kovacs2024Bengal; @Hussain2026Geopolitic]. Governed directly from the imperial capital at Pataliputra, the region enjoyed regular monsoon rainfall exceeding 1.200 mm annually, deep alluvial soils renewed by annual silt deposition, and direct access to rich mineral deposits in the Chota Nagpur plateau, notably iron ore from Singhbhum and copper from the copper belt [@Dwivedi2019Early].

Prachya sustained the highest total population and aggregate demographic mass in the empire, growing from 14,82M in 322BC to 16,15M in 300BC, 17,86M in 260BC and reaching 18,43M in 230BC. Sub-regional density at 260BC stood at 1.900,42 persons per 100 km² (19 persons per km²). Anchored by 3.414 catalogued settlements, the urban network of Prachya was the most sophisticated on the subcontinent, led by Pataliputra (Patna, 320k peak in 260BC), Varanasi (65k peak in 300BC), Kaushambi (62k peak in 300BC), Mathura (50,5k peak in 185BC), Shravasti (46,4k peak in 322BC) and Ayodhya (44,2k peak in 185BC), supported by Vaishali (35,5k peak in 322BC), Champa (Bhagalpur, 32,2k peak in 322BC), Ahichhatra (31,5k peak in 185BC), the fortified regional deltaic capital of Mahasthangarh (Pundranagara, 27,3k peak in 185BC) in northern Bengal, Chandraketugarh (27,3k peak in 185BC), Rajgir (26,9k peak in 322BC) and the maritime outlet of Tamralipti (26,8k peak in 185BC) [@Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Allchin1995Archaeology; @Rashid2020Search].

### Avantiratha (Ujjayini Viceroyalty, Malwa, Gujarat and Rajasthan)

The western viceroyalty of Avantiratha (975.022 km², 24,75% of imperial area) spanned the fertile black cotton soil (*regur*) plateau of Malwa, the river valleys of the Chambal, Narmada and Tapti, the peninsula of Saurashtra and Kathiawar, and the semi-arid grasslands of Rajasthan [@Dwivedi2021Tools]. Administered by a royal viceroy resident at Ujjayini (modern Ujjain), Avantiratha controlled the strategic overland corridors linking the Ganga basin with the western Arabian Sea ports [@Dwivedi2021Political].

Avantiratha supported a population expanding from 6,63M in 322BC to 7,23M in 300BC, 7,99M in 260BC and 8,25M in 230BC, yielding an apex density of 819,47 persons per 100 km². In Saurashtra, Chandragupta's governor (*rashtriya*) Pushyagupta initiated the construction of the famous Sudarshana reservoir near Junagadh, subsequently expanded under Ashoka by the Yavana governor Tushaspha, who added irrigation conduit canals that transformed the surrounding arid coastal plain into productive agricultural land. Among 1.440 catalogued settlements in the province, major urban centres included Ujjayini (Ujjain, 70,6k peak in 185BC; 66,9k in 260BC), Vidisha (Besnagar, 35,3k peak in 185BC), the port emporium of Bharuch (Bhrigukachha, Barygaza, 28,8k peak in 185BC), Junagadh (16,3k peak in 185BC) and Nagari (Madhyamika) [@Allchin1995Archaeology].

### Kalinga (Tosali Viceroyalty and Mahanadi Delta)

The coastal province of Kalinga (153.729 km², 3,9% of imperial area) occupied the maritime corridor along the Bay of Bengal, extending from the Baitarani River south to the Godavari delta, with its demographic nucleus centred on the fertile alluvial delta of the Mahanadi [@Yule2008Early; @Acharjaya2026Historical]. Annexed by Ashoka around 261BC in a campaign whose violence, according to Rock Edict XIII, resulted in the capture of 150.000 persons, the slaying of 100.000 and the death of many times that number from starvation and disease, Kalinga was reorganised under two administrative seats: a northern capital at Tosali (Dhauli) and a southern headquarters at Samapa (Jaugada) [@Yule2009Sisupalgar].

Despite its compact geographical extent, Kalinga exhibited the highest population density of any Mauryan province, supported by intensive double-cropping of wet-rice in the delta, rich estuarine fisheries, and active maritime commerce across the Bay of Bengal to Southeast Asia [@Mishra2026Coastal; @Mukherjee2025Ekamra]. Population rose from 3,12M in 322BC to 3,4M in 300BC, 3,76M at conquest in 260BC, and 3,88M in 230BC, achieving an extraordinary density of 2.445,86 persons per 100 km² (24,46 persons per km²). Across 377 catalogued settlements in Kalinga, the square fortified city of Sisupalgarh near Bhubaneswar (35k peak in 260BC), with its massive clay and brick ramparts, monolithic stone gateways and internal gridded street plan, functioned as the premier urban centre of the delta [@Yule2009Sisupalgar].

### Dakshinapatha (Suvarnagiri Viceroyalty and Peninsular South)

The southern viceroyalty of Dakshinapatha (777.163 km², 19,73% of imperial area) encompassed the Deccan volcanic plateau, the Godavari and Krishna-Tungabhadra basins, the red soil zones of Karnataka, and the Andhra coastal plain [@Shinde2026Autonomous]. Ruled by a viceregal prince headquartered at Suvarnagiri ('Golden Mountain', near modern Jonnagiri in Andhra Pradesh), Dakshinapatha represented a frontier resource zone rich in gold deposits from the Hutti and Kolar reefs, diamond fields in the lower Krishna, and iron ore [@Dwivedi2021Territoria].

Population in Dakshinapatha expanded from 7,02M in 322BC to 7,65M in 300BC, 8,46M in 260BC and peaked at 8,73M in 230BC, with a density of 1.088,57 persons per 100 km² at the Ashokan apex. Rather than direct administrative colonisation, Mauryan authority in the peninsula operated through an enclave model, exercising firm control over mineral extracting districts and arterial routes while leaving inland tribal polities (*atavikas*) and southern kingdoms (Cholas, Pandyas, Satiyaputras and Keralaputras) in autonomous treaty relations [@Shinde2026Autonomous; @Neelakantan2025Digital]. Across 2.084 catalogued settlements, prominent urban centres included Paithan (Pratishthana, 25,3k peak in 185BC), Amaravati (21k peak in 185BC) on the lower Krishna, the western Arabian Sea port of Sopara (Shurparaka, 20,2k peak in 185BC), Sannati in the Bhima valley, and early peninsular towns such as Kanchipuram (18,7k peak in 185BC) [@Champakalakshmi1996Trade; @Bopearachchi2022Indian].

### Provincial Administrative Hierarchy: Mahamatras, Rajukas and Yuktas

Beneath the viceregal princes (*kumaras*), provincial governance relied upon a hierarchical cadre of civil and judicial officials described in Ashokan inscriptions and Kautilyan manuals [@Dwivedi2021Territoria; @Dwivedi2021Political]. At the divisional level, *pradesikas* toured provincial jurisdictions every three to five years to audit accounts, inspect revenue registers and supervise local magistrates.

In rural districts, judicial and fiscal authority was exercised by *rajukas*, high-ranking officers who, as Ashoka recorded in Pillar Edict IV, were placed in charge of many hundred thousands of people with full discretion over rewards and punishments. Assisted by subordinate revenue accountants (*yuktas*), the *rajukas* conducted land surveys, classified soil fertility, registered property boundaries and settled agrarian property disputes. At the sub-district level, *gopas* supervised clusters of five to ten villages, maintaining detailed census ledgers recording the caste, occupation, cattle holdings and tax obligations of every resident household, while *sthanikas* oversaw quarters containing one-quarter of a rural district.

## Road Networks and Strategic Corridors

Imperial integration depended upon a well-maintained network of royal highways (*rajapatha*) supervised by state officials (*agranomoi*) who erected mileposts (*kosa*) at intervals of ten *stadia* (approximately 1,8 km) and maintained rest houses, wells and banyan shade groves along major thoroughfares [@Rani2026Traditiona; @Davis2018Pilgrimage]. The pre-eminent artery was the grand northern highway, the *Uttarapatha*, which extended over 2.000 km from Pataliputra northwestward through Varanasi, Kaushambi, Mathura, Indraprastha and Taxila to Pushkalavati on the Kabul River, linking the alluvial core directly with Central Asian caravan circuits [@Hussain2026Geopolitic].

A second major arterial route, the *Dakshinapatha*, branched southward from Varanasi and Kaushambi, traversing the Vindhyan gaps to Vidisha, Ujjayini and Maheshwar on the Narmada, before descending into the northern Deccan towards Pratishthana (Paithan) and the Krishna valley [@Rani2026Traditiona]. Coastal routes connected Tamralipti in the Bengal delta through Sisupalgarh in Kalinga to the Krishna-Godavari delta ports, while western routes connected Ujjayini with the maritime ports of Bharuch and Sopara. Fluvial transport complemented overland highways: heavy cargo boats moved bulk grain, timber and stone along the Ganga, Yamuna and Indus, permitting low-cost transit across the empire's agrarian core [@Dwivedi2021Tools].

# Arthashastra Agrarian Administration and Fiscal Extraction

## State-Directed Settlement and Agrarian Expansion (Janapadanivesha)

The demographic and fiscal foundation of the Maurya Empire was governed by the principles of state-directed settlement detailed in the second book of Kautilya's *Arthashastra*, termed *janapadanivesha* (the formation of rural districts) [@Kumar2026Environmen; @Dwivedi2021Political]. Recognising that population constituted the ultimate source of state power and fiscal wealth, the Mauryan administration actively organised the settlement of newly cleared tracts by transplanting agrarian populations from overpopulated urban centres or capturing and relocating populations from subdued frontier regions.

Under the Kautilyan model, new villages (*grama*) were systematically laid out at intervals of one to two *krosas* (approximately 3 to 6 km), each comprising between one hundred and five hundred peasant households, predominantly of the Shudra cultivator class (*karsaka*) [@Kumar2026Environmen]. The state provided virgin agricultural land on favourable terms: fields were granted for life to cultivating tenants, with temporary exemptions from revenue taxes (*parihara*) during initial forest clearance and ditch construction. Settlers received draught cattle, seed grain and agricultural implements as repayable state loans. Cultivators who neglected their assigned allotments faced forfeiture, with the land reassigned to diligent village labourers or village corporate bodies, ensuring that productive potential was constantly maximised.

The physical organisation of new agricultural districts followed a regular territorial hierarchy:
- A fortified administrative capital (*sthaniyya*) at the centre of 800 villages, defended by moats, earthen ramparts and timber stockades.
- A secondary market town (*dronamukha*) at the centre of 400 villages, situated at a river confluence or strategic crossroad.
- A tertiary market centre (*karvatika*) at the centre of 200 villages, serving as a regional grain collection depot.
- A local administrative post (*sangrahana*) at the centre of 10 villages, housing the local treasury, storehouse and revenue clerk.

This four-tiered spatial architecture created an institutional bridge connecting remote rural hamlets with the imperial capital. Granaries (*kosthagara*) constructed at each tier stored emergency reserves of rice, barley, mustard seed and pulses. Under severe famine conditions (*durbhiksha*), the state distributed relief grain from royal storehouses, remitted peasant taxes, and organised public works programmes constructing irrigation canals and dams, as commemorated in the third-century BC Mauryan Brahmi inscription on the limestone plaque found at Mahasthangarh in Bengal and the copper-plate inscription from Sohgaura in Uttar Pradesh [@Rashid2020Search; @Mukhopadhyay2021Ancient].

## Crown Lands (Sita), Communal Cultivation and Land Revenue

The Mauryan agrarian economy operated on a bifurcated land tenure structure that distinguished crown lands (*sita*) from private or communal peasant holdings (*rashtra*) [@Shinde2026King]. Crown lands were managed directly by the state superintendent of agriculture (*sitadhyaksha*). These state domains were worked by three distinct labour forces: indentured labourers (*karmakaras*), enslaved captives (*dasas*), and tenant sharecroppers (*ardhasitikas*) who contributed their own seed and oxen in exchange for half of the harvested yield, or received one-fourth to one-fifth of the crop when relying entirely on state-provided inputs.

On communal peasant lands, agriculturalists held hereditary rights of cultivation subject to the payment of the standard royal share (*bhaga*), traditionally assessed at one-sixth (16,67%) of gross agricultural production, though raised to one-fourth (25%) or one-third in fertile, state-irrigated zones or during periods of fiscal emergency (*pranaya*) [@Shinde2026King; @Mukhopadhyay2021Ancient]. Additional rural levies included the *bali* (religious tithe), *kara* (tax on commercial cash crops such as orchards and sugarcane), and *senabhakta* (provisions for troops marching through the district). By combining direct estate management on crown lands with regular revenue extraction across peasant holdings, the Mauryan fisc commanded unprecedented agricultural surpluses capable of supporting a standing army estimated by Megasthenes at 600.000 infantry, 30.000 cavalry and 9.000 war elephants.

## Irrigation Works (Setubandha) and State Water Administration

Water management was central to Mauryan agronomic policy, classified in the *Arthashastra* as *setubandha* (hydraulic works) [@Kumar2026Environmen]. The treatise distinguished between natural river-fed irrigation works (*sahodaka-setu*) and storage reservoirs constructed by impounding seasonal runoff (*aharyodaka-setu*). The state encouraged private collective investment in irrigation: village communities that constructed tanks, stone dams and watercourses collectively were granted tax exemptions for periods ranging from three to five years depending on the scale of capital expenditure.

Where the state constructed and maintained large-scale irrigation canals and embankments, it levied a specific water rate (*udakabhaga*) scaled according to the lifting mechanism employed:
- One-fifth (20%) of the crop yield for water carried manually in pots.
- One-fourth (25%) for water lifted by bullock-drawn leather buckets (*mohte*) or water-wheels (*arghatta*).
- One-third (33,33%) for water diverted into gravity-fed irrigation channels.
- One-fourth for water elevated from rivers, lakes and natural reservoirs into terraced paddy basins.

The prime archaeological exemplar of Mauryan hydraulic engineering is the Sudarshana dam at Junagadh in the Girnar hills of Gujarat. Epigraphic records of the Western Satrap Rudradaman (150AD) and the Gupta emperor Skandagupta (456AD) explicitly record that this monumental masonry reservoir was founded by Chandragupta Maurya's provincial governor Pushyagupta and subsequently fitted with water-sluices and distribution conduits by Ashoka's governor Tushaspha, proving continuous state management of regional hydraulic systems over centuries.

## Punch-Marked Currency (Karshapana) and Fiscal Extraction

Monetisation under the Mauryas reached a continental scale unmatched in South Asia until the mediaeval period [@Dwivedi2021Tools; @Shinde2026King]. The standard state currency was the silver punch-marked coin (*pana* or *karshapana*), weighing approximately 3,57 grams (32 *rattis*) with a silver content maintained at 75% to 80%, alloyed with copper and trace lead. These irregular rectangular or rounded silver blanks were stamped with five official symbols: the sun symbol, the six-armed symbol (shadara-cakra), a tree-in-railing or hill symbol, and two variable mint or moneyer countermarks [@Mukhopadhyay2021Ancient].

The circulation of *karshapanas* was regulated by the state superintendent of coinage (*lakshanadhyaksha*) and the currency examiner (*rupadarshaka*), who extracted a minting fee (*ruparupa*) of 8% and an assay fee of 5% [@Shinde2026King]. The uniform distribution of identical five-symbol imperial punch-marked coins across hoard sites from Taxila in the north to Amaravati in the south, and from Kandahar to Mahasthangarh in Bengal, demonstrates an integrated monetary sphere that facilitated imperial tax collection, military payrolls, and market transactions across vast geographic distances.

## Forest Polities (Atavika) and Frontier Integration

Beyond the settled agrarian villages lay extensive tracts of tropical forest and scrub savanna inhabited by autonomous forest tribes (*atavika* or *aranyaka*) [@Kumar2026Environmen; @Shinde2026King]. Kautilya recognised these forest domains as both a strategic defence barrier and a reservoir of critical state resources, particularly timber for river fleets, medicinal aromatics, and war elephants captured from sanctuaries in Kalinga, Magadha and Assam under the supervision of the superintendent of elephants (*hastyadhyaksha*).

Rather than enforcing violent conquest, Ashoka adopted a policy of pacification and moral suasion towards the forest peoples. In Major Rock Edict XIII, the emperor explicitly addressed the forest tribes, declaring that even in his remorse following Kalinga, "the Beloved of the Gods possesses power, and the forest tribes are bidden to turn from evil ways that they may not be slain." The state maintained a specialised intelligence corps of forest wardens (*atavikapalas*) and recruited tribal warriors as auxiliary scouts (*atavibala*), integrating frontier populations as buffer communities along imperial margins.

# Material Culture, Urbanism and Epigraphic Networks

## Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW) and Urban Nucleation

The material culture of the Maurya period is defined archaeologically by the widespread distribution of Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW), a deluxe ceramic tradition characterised by an exceptionally lustrous, mirror-like black, golden or silvery surface finish produced via reduction firing and the application of an iron-rich slip [@Hawkes2020Back; @Dwivedi2019Early; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation]. Originating in the middle Ganga valley during the sixth century BC, NBPW expanded rapidly between 350BC and 200BC across the subcontinent, tracking the administrative expansion of the Mauryan state from Taxila and Charsadda in the northwest to Amaravati, Sisupalgarh and Mahasthangarh in the south and east.

Excavations at Bhir Mound (Taxila), Kaushambi, Rajghat (Varanasi), Prahladpur, Vaishali, Pataliputra and Sisupalgarh reveal that the NBPW horizon corresponded with monumental brick architecture, paved drains, soak pits lined with terracotta ring-wells, and standardised terracotta figurines [@Hawkes2020Back]. The adoption of terracotta ring-wells permitted dense residential nucleation within city walls by providing deep household water access and domestic sanitary drainage, directly overcoming urban disease vectors that had constrained earlier second-millennium BC settlements.

## Monumental Epigraphy and Ashokan Edicts

The most explicit spatial footprint of Mauryan imperial authority is preserved in Ashoka's monumental epigraphic corpus, comprising fourteen Major Rock Edicts, two Separate Kalinga Edicts, seven Major Pillar Edicts, and numerous Minor Rock Edicts inscribed in stone across thirty-nine distinct geographical locations [@Davis2018Pilgrimage; @Wick2013Religions]. The linguistic geography of the edicts reveals a sophisticated provincial communication strategy:
- Prakrit written in Brahmi script was employed across the vast majority of central, eastern and peninsular sites.
- Prakrit in Kharoshthi script was utilised on northwestern rock faces at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra, reflecting regional scribal traditions derived from Aramaic.
- Greek and Aramaic bilingual inscriptions were carved at Kandahar (Shar-i-Kuna) and Taxila, directly addressing Hellenised and Iranian-speaking frontier populations [@Fauconnier2015Occidente].

The spatial placement of Ashokan edicts reflects a deliberate cartographic design: Major Rock Edicts were carved on prominent granite and basalt boulders along peripheral frontier boundaries (Kandahar, Girnar, Sopara, Dhauli, Jaugada, Erragudi, Kalsi), marking the territorial limits of the imperial domain, whereas polished sandstone Pillar Edicts were erected at major urban nodes, pilgrim shrines and river crossings along the central Ganga valley (Sarnath, Sanchi, Vaishali, Lauriya-Nandangarh, Rampurva, Meerut, Topra) [@Davis2018Pilgrimage].

## Commercial Guilds (Shreni) and Long-Distance Exchange

Long-distance commerce in the Maurya Empire was organised through corporate merchant and artisan guilds (*shreni* and *nigama*), which maintained their own customary laws (*shrenidharma*), exercised civil jurisdiction over members, and minted regional token currencies [@Dwivedi2021Tools; @Dwivedi2021Territoria]. The state regulated guild activities through the superintendent of commerce (*panyadhyaksha*), who fixed standard commodity prices, inspected weights and measures stamped by the superintendent of metrology (*pautavadhyaksha*), and levied transit tolls (*shulka*) of one-twentieth (5%) to one-tenth (10%) at city customs gates [@Mukhopadhyay2021Ancient].

Guilds coordinated extensive cross-continental trade:
- Fine cotton textiles from Varanasi and Bengal, silk imports from China, and muslins from Kalinga moved westward along the *Uttarapatha*.
- Spikenard, costus, lapis lazuli and horses from Central Asia entered northwestern markets through Taxila.
- Black pepper, sandalwood, pearls and beryl from peninsular South India moved north along the *Dakshinapatha* towards the Ganga capitals.
- Maritime trade through Bharuch and Sopara connected the subcontinent with the Persian Gulf, South Arabia and Ptolemaic Egypt [@Bopearachchi2022Indian; @Eshel2024Thousand].

Under Kautilyan commercial jurisprudence, corporate guilds functioned as financial institutions, accepting perpetual interest-bearing deposits (*akshayanivi*) from royal patrons and wealthy merchants to endow charitable feeding halls, hospitals and religious shrines [@Dwivedi2021Political]. Guilds pooled capital through joint commercial ventures (*sambhuya-samutthana*), underwriting overland merchant caravans (*sartha*) of hundreds of bullock carts and financing maritime voyages across the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea. This sophisticated corporate commercial apparatus generated substantial transit customs revenues (*shulka*) for the imperial treasury while sustaining extensive inter-provincial economic integration throughout the empire.

# Methodological Framework and Spatial Calibration

## Raster Disaggregation and Environmental Covariates

To distribute historical population across the 3.938.787 km² land area of the Maurya Empire, the INDUS spatial engine partitions the continental domain into 51.246 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells. Each cell is evaluated against environmental covariates calibrated to ancient South Asian agrarian realities:
- Alluvial soil fertility: binary and continuous weights prioritising quaternary river alluvium across the Indo-Gangetic and deltaic tracts over crystalline shield soils.
- Monsoon rainfall isohyets: scaling carrying capacity based on annual precipitation gradients, distinguishing wet paddy zones (> 1.200 mm) from semi-arid millet-wheat zones (< 600 mm).
- Fluvial proximity: exponential decay weighting based on distance to perennial navigable rivers (Ganga, Yamuna, Indus, Narmada, Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi), reflecting domestic water availability, irrigation access and transport advantages.
- Terrain ruggedness: penalising mountainous escarpments in the Western Ghats, Vindhyas and Himalayas exceeding 15% slope.

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Baselines

To eliminate double-counting between nucleated urban centres and rural cultivators, 9.518 catalogued settlements with chronological population series are directly anchored to their WGS84 geographic coordinates. At each benchmark year, the active population of all catalogued settlements within a provincial domain is summed and subtracted from the provincial demographic envelope.

The remaining rural population is subsequently distributed across non-settled pixels in proportion to environmental suitability weights. A two-pass boundary smoothing filter feathers density gradients across provincial borders, preventing artificial density cliffs along administrative borders.

## Demographic Uncertainty Envelopes

Every provincial and imperial benchmark estimate carries an explicit symmetric uncertainty bound (+/- 8% across all benchmark years from 322BC to 185BC). At the imperial apex in 260BC, the headline population of 47M is bounded between 43,24M and 50,76M inhabitants. This uncertainty interval accommodates variance across competing archaeological house-size estimates, excavation sample coverage and text-based army multiplier estimates [@Hawkes2020Back; @Dwivedi2019Trends].

Sensitivity analyses evaluate competing assumptions regarding the urban-rural population split. Intramural residential densities across excavated NBPW cities are modelled at 120 to 180 persons per hectare, derived from house-floor area measurements at Bhir Mound and Kaushambi [@Hawkes2020Back]. Rural densities across the Indo-Gangetic alluvium range between 15 and 35 persons per km², reflecting double-cropped paddy agriculture and riverine fishing. The symmetric 8% uncertainty interval accounts for potential under-enumeration of seasonal pastoralist populations in the Thar and Baluchistan, as well as shifting swidden cultivators in the Vindhyan and Eastern Ghats forests.

## Historical Demographic Phases

### Foundation and Unification under Chandragupta (322BC to 300BC)

The establishment of the Maurya dynasty commenced around 322BC when Chandragupta Maurya, guided by his chief advisor Kautilya (Chanakya), mobilised discontented populations in the Punjab and northwestern frontiers to overthrow the unpopular Nanda dynasty of Magadha [@Fauconnier2015Occidente; @Hussain2026Geopolitic]. Capturing Pataliputra, Chandragupta inherited a wealthy, highly nucleated state controlling the middle and lower Ganga valley.

Between 305BC and 303BC, Chandragupta confronted Seleucus I Nicator, who sought to recover Alexander's Indian satrapies. The resulting treaty established a dynastic alliance, secured 500 war elephants for Seleucus, and annexed the four eastern satrapies of Paropamisadae (Kabul), Arachosia (Kandahar), Gedrosia (Baluchistan) and Aria (Herat) to the Mauryan crown [@Fauconnier2015Occidente; @Morris2019Central]. Over this initial period, imperial population expanded from 39M in 322BC to 42,5M by 300BC, reflecting political pacification, the suppression of banditry along trunk routes, and the commencement of state-directed agrarian colonisation in the Doab.

### Peninsular Expansion under Bindusara (300BC to 273BC)

Under Chandragupta's successor Bindusara (Amitraghata, 'Slayer of Foes'), who reigned from approximately 297BC to 273BC, Mauryan arms pushed southward across the Vindhyan divide into the Deccan plateau and peninsular South India [@Shinde2026Autonomous]. Tibetan and Jain chronicles credit Bindusara and his minister Chanakya with subduing sixteen states between the eastern and western oceans, establishing the viceregal seat of Suvarnagiri in Karnataka and absorbing the northern Deccan up to the frontiers of the Tamil kingdoms.

This southward expansion brought the rich goldfields of Karnataka and the maritime outlets of the Konkan and Andhra coasts into the imperial economic orbit. Imperial population expanded at an annual rate of 0,33%, reaching approximately 45,5M by the end of Bindusara's reign, with substantial growth occurring in Avantiratha and Dakshinapatha as commercial contacts between the north and south multiplied.

### Ashokan Zenith, Kalinga Integration and Dhamma Administration (273BC to 232BC)

Following a contested succession after Bindusara's death, Ashoka ascended the throne of Pataliputra around 269BC. In the eighth year of his consecration (ca. 261BC), Ashoka launched the fateful invasion of Kalinga, conquering the independent coastal kingdom and incorporating Tosali into the imperial provincial structure [@Yule2008Early; @Acharjaya2026Historical].

The demographic consequences of the Kalinga war transformed Ashokan governance. Profoundly affected by the slaughter and deportation of civilian populations, Ashoka renounced aggressive territorial conquest (*digvijaya*) in favour of moral conquest through righteousness (*dhammavijaya*) [@Davis2018Pilgrimage; @Wick2013Religions]. Over the subsequent three decades, the emperor established the office of morality commissioners (*dhammamahamatras*), prohibited animal sacrifices, established state hospitals (*chikitsa*) for humans and animals, and planted medicinal herbs and shade trees throughout the provinces.

Under this prolonged era of internal peace and administrative stability, the imperial population reached 47M at 260BC and peaked at 48,5M around 230BC. Aggregate density attained 1.231,34 persons per 100 km² across the 3,94M km² empire. Urban centres flourished: Pataliputra, described by Megasthenes as an enclosed rectangle 80 *stadia* (14,8 km) long and 15 *stadia* (2,8 km) wide protected by 570 towers and 64 gates, reached 320k residents at 260BC, while Ujjayini (66,9k in 260BC; 70,6k peak in 185BC), Varanasi (63,8k in 260BC; 65k peak in 300BC), Kaushambi (59,9k in 260BC; 62k peak in 300BC), Taxila (53,6k in 260BC; 59,1k peak in 185BC) and Sisupalgarh (35k in 260BC) anchored provincial exchange networks [@Yule2009Sisupalgar; @Allchin1995Archaeology].

### Post-Ashokan Decentralisation and Sunga Transition (232BC to 185BC)

Following the death of Ashoka around 232BC, the Maurya Empire experienced rapid political decentralisation and territorial fragmentation [@Dwivedi2019Early]. Dynastic traditions record that the empire was partitioned between Ashoka's grandsons Dasharatha (ruling the eastern provinces from Pataliputra) and Kunala or Samprati (ruling the western viceroyalties from Ujjayini). Lacking strong central authority, distant provinces gradually seceded:
- In the northwest, Greco-Bactrian rulers under Demetrius advanced across the Hindu Kush into Gandhara and Punjab.
- In the Deccan, local rulers and the emerging Satavahana dynasty asserted independence.
- In Kalinga, the Chedi dynasty under Kharavela established an autonomous kingdom by the late second century BC.

The imperial population receded from its peak of 48,5M in 230BC to 46,5M by 185BC, when the last Mauryan ruler, Brihadratha, was assassinated during a military parade by his commander-in-chief, Pushyamitra Sunga, who established the Sunga dynasty in Magadha. Despite political fragmentation, the underlying agricultural infrastructure, urban networks and commercial guild institutions established during the Mauryan era persisted into the post-Mauryan period.

# Settlement Systems and Gazetteer Synthesis

The INDUS settlement database catalogues 9.518 georeferenced archaeological and historical settlements across the Maurya Empire, reconciling primary-monograph city trajectories, archaeological survey corpora, monument inventories, official census baselines and historical toponymy across five provincial submasks: Prachya and Imperial Core (3.414 settlements), Uttarapatha (2.203), Dakshinapatha (2.084), Avantiratha (1.440) and Kalinga (377) [@Allchin1995Archaeology; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making; @ImperialGazetteer1908]. Across the 9.518-settlement corpus, the log-log rank-size distribution fits a Zipf slope of $\alpha = 0,87$ ($R^2 = 0,95$), confirming a primate-dominated imperial urban hierarchy anchored by Pataliputra and supported by a dense secondary tier of provincial capitals and market *qasbas* [@Habib1982Atlas; @Hambly1982Towns]. Table \ref{tab:leading_settlements} presents the leading urban settlements ordered by peak demographic scale.

The urban hierarchy was dominated by the imperial capital of Pataliputra (Patna, 320k peak in 260BC), situated at the strategic confluence of the Ganga, Son, Gandak and Ghaghara rivers [@Allchin1995Archaeology; @Hambly1982Towns; @Naqvi1968Urbanisation]. Beneath Patna, the top eight imperial metropolises comprised Ujjain (Ujjayini, 70,6k peak in 185BC), Varanasi (65k peak in 300BC), Kaushambi (62k peak in 300BC), Taxila (59,1k peak in 185BC), Mathura (50,5k peak in 185BC), Shravasti (46,4k peak in 322BC) and Ayodhya (44,2k peak in 185BC) [@Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Bayly1983Rulers]. Along the northwestern corridors of Uttarapatha, Taxila was flanked by Charsadda (Pushkalavati, 35,6k peak), Sialkot (34,1k peak), Delhi (Indraprastha, 28,1k peak), Multan (24,4k peak) and Peshawar (19,2k peak) [@Morris2019Evidence; @Blake1991Shahjahanabad].

In Avantiratha, Ujjain was supported by Vidisha (35,3k peak in 185BC) and the Arabian Sea emporium of Bharuch (28,8k peak in 185BC), while Kalinga was anchored by the fortified square stronghold of Sisupalgarh (35k peak in 260BC) [@Yule2009Sisupalgar]. Within Prachya and the eastern delta, secondary centres included Vaishali (35,5k), Bhagalpur (32,2k), Ahichhatra (31,5k), Mahasthangarh (27,3k) in northern Bengal, Chandraketugarh (27,3k), Rajgir (26,9k) and the maritime outlet of Tamralipti (26,8k) [@Rashid2020Search; @Eaton1993Rise]. Across Dakshinapatha, Paithan (25,3k), Amaravati (21k), Sopara (20,2k) and Kanchipuram (18,7k) coordinated Deccan and peninsular exchange [@Champakalakshmi1996Trade; @Stein1989Vijayanagara].

By coupling 9.518 georeferenced settlement trajectories with spatial kriging and environmental suitability covariates, INDUS establishes a realistic demographic reconstruction of ancient South Asia's first continental empire.
